title: How are old places different from new places? A psychological investigation of the correlation between patina, spontaneous fantasies, and place attachment
research_focus: To understand 'age value' by investigating the fundamental differences in experience and affect between old and new urban residential places, specifically how physical age, patina, and spontaneous fantasies correlate with place attachment.

sample_context.description: Four males and three females from historic Charleston and two males and three females from I'On, aged approximately 25 to 75 years. Participants were part-time residents of either neighborhood, familiar with it, and regularly walked in it. This was a purposeful sample.
sample_context.setting: Historic Charleston, South Carolina (an authentically 'old' place) and I'On, Mount Pleasant, South Carolina (a 'new' urbanist development).

findings.antecedent: layered townscape elements (buildings, fountains, fences, walls, gates, vegetation)
findings.source: Phase one results: the qualitative experience of historic Charleston and I'On and spontaneous fantasy, page 11
findings.description: Informants from both historic Charleston and I'On described their neighborhoods as composed of discrete, layered elements (buildings, fountains, iron fences, masonry walls, ornamental gates, vegetation). This layered quality created a strong sense of discovery and mystery, prompting a desire to explore the neighborhood.

findings.consequent: perception of unseen human effort in maintenance
findings.source: Phase one results: the qualitative experience of historic Charleston and I'On and spontaneous fantasy, page 13
findings.description: Informants from both historic Charleston and I'On sensed the significant unseen effort required to maintain the beautiful gardens and houses in their neighborhoods. This perception was unselfconscious and not tied to property value, but rather a feeling of goodness about being in a place where people expend effort to maintain quality.
supporting_quotes: people care about their homes and yards and are willing to spend great effort in their upkeep in maintenance

findings.consequent: creation of stories about the past
findings.source: Phase one results: the qualitative experience of historic Charleston and I'On and spontaneous fantasy, page 13
findings.description: Informants from historic Charleston (but not I'On) described deciphering the age of various landscape and building layers, mentally 'peeling back' them to create a story about the past, akin to reading pages of a book.

findings.antecedent: aged landscape or building element (patina, decay)
findings.source: Phase one results: the qualitative experience of historic Charleston and I'On and spontaneous fantasy, page 13
findings.description: Informants from historic Charleston uniquely experienced spontaneous fantasies, where an image or vignette from the past spontaneously appeared in their minds' eye upon encountering an appropriately decayed object in the right environmental context. This experience was unconscious, highly emotional, and helped bond them to the place.
supporting_quotes: This is Longitude Lane. What I like about it is you can see the wagon ruts coming down.
imagined Civil War soldiers marching up and down the steps.
There's this old city that's now inhabited by monkeys, but it's half vegetation and half old stones.

supporting_quotes_or_evidence_snippets: This is Longitude Lane. What I like about it is you can see the wagon ruts coming down. The docks were right off from there, they would load them up when the ships came up.

You get a feeling that ... something is happening that's bigger than our little moment and you're kind of glimpsing some future where that could be a possible, you know, we're now going to the jungle or maybe not.
mechanism_candidates: Spontaneous fantasy is catalysed by encountering an aged landscape or building element, requiring both a positive valuation of patina and cognitive engagement in 'reading' the environment.
Patina and decay appear necessary for an historic environment to feel authentic, which then enables spontaneous fantasies and emotional attachment.
transferability_limits: The purposeful sample was designed to collect relevant meanings to inform the survey instrument and thus the results are not directly generalizable to the broader population.
Findings are specific to the unique contexts of Historic Charleston and I'On, which share similar urban design but differ significantly in age.
limitations: The purposeful sample for the qualitative phase limits generalizability to the broader population.
The R² value in the quantitative phase indicated a low amount of variation in how respondents answered place attachment questions, suggesting other unmeasured factors may be at play.
Further research is needed to establish the optimal balance between decay and patina to maximize emotional attachment to place.
